newsitem.title: UK: BoE to quote gilts in decimals from next year.
newsitem.headline: BoE to quote gilts in decimals from next year.

text.p: The Bank of England said on Monday it will quote gilt prices in decimals rather than 32nds from next year.
"Almost all major international bond markets use decimal prices. the United States is the only other exception," the Bank said in a statement.

The implementation date will be set after consultation with market participants and will take account of the implications for firms' systems and for the specification of LIFFE gilt contracts. "The change will not be implemented before April 1998," it said.

The Bank said a large majority of those who responded to a consultation paper favoured such a change. They also backed a move to change the "daycount convention" used for the calculation of accrued interest on government bonds.
"The majority of those responding to the paper wished to switch from the actual/365 to the actual/actual convention," it said.

That means semi-annual coupon payments will be calculated on the actual number of days covered by the coupon rather than 182.5 days -- half a calendar year. This change will also be made next year, the Bank said.

"The change of convention builds on the recommendations of the Report of the Working Group on the Gilts Market after EMU and is consistent with the recommendations of the Bank's Working Group on Market Conventions in London Financial Markets," the statement said.
The Bank also invited views on what formula should be adopted to allow gilt strips to trade on a yield basis.
A majority favoured a method involving compound interest for all strips, including the shortest, on an actual/actual basis. There was a preference for adjusting for non-working days.
"The Bank therefore proposes that this be the pricing method for strips from the start of the strips market," it said.
The date for the start of the strips market will be announced later this summer but is expected to be in late September or October.

The Bank also took soundings on possible changes to the ex-dividend period. A large majority of those responding favoured the proposal to abolish the ex-dividend period for gilts held in the Central Gilts Office.

It was recognised that there would need to be changes to arrangements for trading gilts between CGO members and gilt holders outside CGO or holders on the National Savings Stock Register, where the ex-dividend period could only be reduced from seven to five working days.

A large majority also favoured the abolition of both the special ex- and special cum-dividend facilities. No decision has yet been made on whether to proceed with these changes, which would require secondary legislation and any change would not come before April 1998, the Bank said.
